summary: For 5–6 year-olds learning local weather patterns, the core skill is procedural: children gather their own daily weather observations with agreed picture symbols, record them over days and weeks on a visible chart or pictograph, then READ the accumulated record together to describe simple patterns (e.g. 'more rainy days than sunny days this week') and make a simple, tentative prediction grounded in that record. The goal is descriptive, not explanatory — no causes of weather yet. The main activity is an ongoing record-and-read routine; vocabulary priming and reading a pre-made pictograph are useful scaffolds with stated limits.
misconceptions: Thinking a single day's weather represents the whole season or that 'today = always'.
Confusing weather (what it's doing now) with season, or expecting weather to be identical every day.
Reading a pictograph by counting the wrong thing (e.g. the shortest column) or ignoring that each symbol stands for one day.
Believing weather is fully predictable, or conversely totally random with no patterns.
Recording what they wish the weather was rather than what they observe.

activities.title: Daily weather station: record over time, then read your own chart
steps: Each day, look outside and choose today's weather symbol(s) from an agreed set: sun, cloud, rain, wind, snow. To tell if it is sunny, look at shadows on the ground (sharp shadows mean sunshine) and the overall daylight — never look directly at the sun.
Add a simple warm/cold marker (is it warm or cold today?).
Place that day's entry onto a growing weekly chart or pictograph so a column builds up for each weather type.
At the end of the week, step back and READ the chart: which column is tallest? Say the pattern aloud — e.g. 'this week was more rainy than sunny.'

Use the pattern to make a simple prediction about tomorrow, and say what on the chart makes you think so (e.g. 'it's been rainy most days, so maybe rainy again') — keeping it a guess, not a certainty.
Keep the routine going into a new week and compare: did the pattern change?
Link the record to the current season so weather observation and seasonal knowledge reinforce each other.
activities.insight: A pattern emerges from many observations collected over time; children can describe what their own data shows, and base a simple prediction on it, rather than being told a fact.

activities.title: Weather-symbol vocabulary primer
steps: Explore an illustrated sky scene and tap or point to each weather type.
Hear and say its name (sunny, cloudy, rainy, windy, snowy) and see its matching symbol.
Match each weather symbol to its spoken name before starting the weather diary.
activities.insight: Children learn the shared vocabulary and symbols for weather types so they can record consistently later.

activities.title: Read a finished weather pictograph
steps: Look at a simple pre-made weather pictograph of a week.
Answer aloud: which column is tallest? Were there more rainy or sunny days?
Match weather symbols to their names.
activities.insight: Reading a completed pictograph means checking what each symbol stands for (in this chart, one symbol = one day), then comparing column heights, which works when the symbols are the same size and evenly spaced, or counting the symbols in each column.

checkQuestion: Over a week or two, ask the child to observe the weather each day and record it on a simple chart (sunny/cloudy/rainy, warm/cold, windy). Then ask them to point out any pattern and predict tomorrow. Watch how they observe, record consistently, and read their own chart — don't ask them to define 'weather.'
checkAnswer: Records each day's conditions consistently with clear symbols or words, keeps it going over time, spots a simple pattern (e.g. 'it's been rainy all week,' 'colder in the mornings') and makes a sensible prediction grounded in the recent record.
